description.narrative: MyRight arbetar med att stärka funktionsrättsrörelsen i Bosnien och Hercegovina, med särskilt fokus på dess förmåga att påverka beslutsfattare på olika nivåer att säkerställa rättigheter för människor med funktionsvariation. MyRight samarbetar med en mängd olika partnerorganisationer i landet som är samlade i fem så kallade koalitioner. Det här projektet syftar till att öka deltagandet för kvinnor och flickor med funktionsvariation i funktionsrättsrörelsen och att stärka dem att ta större plats, engagera sig och påverka. De fem koalitionerna och deras respektive medlemsorganisationer kommer att utbildas kring jämställdhet och jämställdhetsintegrering och strukturer kommer att byggas upp kring hur kvinnor och flickor kan ta större plats i organisationerna. De fem koalitionerna är direkt involverade i att ta fram och genomföra projektet, och kommer med svenska biståndspengar att få finansiellt stöd från MyRight för sitt arbete.

MyRight works to strengthen the disability rights movement in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a special focus on its ability to influence decision-makers at various levels to ensure the rights of persons with disabilities. MyRight collaborates with a variety of partner organizations in the country that are united in five so-called coalitions. This project aims to increase the participation of women and girls with disabilities in the disability rights movement, and to strengthen them to get involved and influence the work of the disability rights movement. The five coalitions and their respective member organizations will be trained on gender equality and gender mainstreaming, and structures will be built around how to increase participation and influence of women and girls with disabilities in the organizations. The five coalitions are directly involved in developing and implementing the project, and will, with Swedish development aid funds, receive financial support from MyRight for their work.

The long term goal of the project is to improve the implementation of the rights of women and girls with disabilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Expected outcomes: 1. Increased participation of women and girls with disabilities within organisations of persons with disabilities 2.Women and girls with disabilities are empowered to have, to a greater extent, the power to shape activities in the disabilitiy movement The theory of change can be summarized as if OPDs have a better understanding of gender equality, they will also better understand what kind of support is needed for women and girls to increase their involvement. This will, in turn, increase the likeliness of women and girls participating to a greater extent than today and lead to a strengthening of the work promoting their rights.

Key Results: Empowerment and Participation: More than 100 WWDs who were previously excluded now actively participate in organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs). Through mentoring, human rights education, and structured Forums, women have strengthened their confidence, leadership, and advocacy skills. Forums provided safe spaces for solidarity and learning, and membership has more than doubled since their establishment. Women have initiated advocacy actions at local and cantonal levels, including inclusive health services, vocational education, and personal assistance.
Policy and Structural Change: Thirty-three OPDs adopted the first-ever Rulebook on Prevention and Protection from Gender-Based and Sexual Violence, embedding gender equality into organizational practices. Forums are recognized as platforms for rights-based advocacy, influencing OPD policies and local government decisions.
Representation and Voice: Before the project, WWDs rights were rarely visible in OPD advocacy. Today, women themselves advocate for health, employment, accessibility, and equality. Communities and institutions increasingly recognize WWDs voices and contributions. WWDs are significantly more visible and vocal within OPDs and local communities compared to four years ago.
Sustainability: WWDs have gained lasting knowledge and skills, but continued support is essential to prevent regression. Forums have proven successful and should be expanded nationwide to maintain momentum. MyRights expertise in bridging disability and gender equality strengthened local ownership and embedded inclusive practices into OPDs.
Remaining Challenges: OPDs need to move beyond declarations and integrate gender equality into leadership, programs, and budgets. Womens rights movements must fully include WWDs as women first, ensuring accessibility and meaningful participation. Financial and accessibility barriers persist.
Conclusion: The project has significantly advanced the rights and visibility of WWDs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, laying a strong foundation for sustainable inclusion and advocacy. Continued investment is critical to maintain progress and expand impact.
